name: NonuniformFFTs.jl (Julia NUFFT, CPU and GPU) vs FINUFFT and cuFINUFFT
baseline: FINUFFT v2.4.1 (C++, CPU) and cuFINUFFT (CUDA C++, GPU), both compiled locally and called through FINUFFT.jl v3.4.0
workload: Type-1 and type-2 3D non-uniform FFTs on a uniform 256^3 grid, random points in [0, 2*pi)^3 with point density N/M^3 from 1e-4 to 10, tolerance 1e-6, Float64 complex data; each time includes set_points plus the transform.
claimed_speedup: README: on CPU 'comparable performance' to FINUFFT (no CPU win claimed); on GPU it 'can be faster than the CUDA-based CuFINUFFT, especially for large problem sizes'. Docs: the default global-memory GPU method is 'slightly faster than CuFINUFFT at low point densities, but slightly slower at large ones'; the non-default shared-memory method gives 'important gains with respect to the CuFINUFFT implementation' at large densities. The gains appear only in plots; no numeric ratio is printed on either page.
compiler_and_flags: FINUFFT built with Nvidia nvc++ via CMake 'Release' with default flags (FFTW.ESTIMATE, spread_sort=1, spread_kerevalmeth=1, tolerance 1e-6, modeord=1); cuFINUFFT built with nvcc from CUDA 12.8 and CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90; NonuniformFFTs.jl v0.8.3 (2025-07-11) on Julia with KernelAbstractions.jl/CUDA.jl (Julia version not stated on the page). Script: benchmark/CPU+CUDA/run_benchmarks.jl.
hardware: Jean Zay (IDRIS): 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 (24 cores used) and one NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB (1/4 of a node). A second run on one AMD Instinct MI300A (Adastra) compares only the CPU against FINUFFT.
why_faster: Docs, GPU only and hedged: the shared-memory variant 'completely avoids atomic operations on shared memory', which 'seems to speed up things quite a bit and might explain the important gains' over cuFINUFFT. The implementation is described as 'heavily inspired' by the cuFINUFFT paper, so the algorithm family is the same but not identical.
tradeoffs: Julia package; one KernelAbstractions.jl code base targets CUDA, AMD and other GPUs. Also offers real-valued non-uniform data transforms (extra gains, not available in FINUFFT).
caveats: Author's own benchmark, results only as SVG plots with no numeric table. The CPU result is parity, not a win. The GPU win is regime dependent: the default method is slower than cuFINUFFT at high density and the faster shared-memory method has to be chosen. The 'real data' gains solve a different (real-valued) problem. On AMD GPUs the default method scales badly. Only one GPU model (H100) and one tolerance (1e-6) were tested, and the Julia compiler version is not stated.

name: SymbolicUtils.jl / Symbolics.jl (Julia symbolic engine) vs SymEngine (C++): SciMLBenchmarks SymEngineComparison
baseline: SymEngine v0.12.0 (C++ symbolic library, via SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 and SymEngine_jll)
workload: Ten symbolic workloads adapted from SymEngine's own C++ benchmark suite plus SymbolicUtils-native ones: diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term Taylor series, trig-product substitution, 10^5-draw random-expression substitution (dense and sparse rule), variable search on shared and unshared expression sets, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, code-generation init, and the call of the generated function with common-subexpression elimination.
claimed_speedup: SymbolicUtils is faster than SymEngine in 4 of 10 rows (SymEngine s vs SymbolicUtils s): compiled call with CSE 6.93256e-7 vs 3.13135e-7 (2.2x), variable search on dissimilar expressions 4.67036e-4 vs 2.13078e-4 (2.2x), variable search on common subtrees 1.02663e-3 vs 4.89876e-4 (2.1x), substitution of a 10^5-draw expression with a sparse rule 1.10077e-3 vs 5.92595e-4 (1.9x) (ratios derived from page data). SymEngine is faster in the other 6: diff of expand 6.95691e-3 vs 0.332787 (SymbolicUtils 48x slower), eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0116745 vs 0.331982 (28x), codegen init 1.15092e-3 vs 1.34645e-2 (12x), series 1.99123e-3 vs 1.98982e-2 (10x), trig-product substitution 1.478e-5 vs 6.0009e-5 (4.1x), dense-rule substitution 1.13195e-3 vs 3.95472e-3 (3.5x).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8, znver2), SymbolicUtils v4.46.6, Symbolics v7.39.2, SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 with the prebuilt SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0 binary (its compiler and flags are not stated); timings are minimum over samples (Chairmarks). Source: SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd.
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (128 virtual cores), Linux x86_64 CI runner
why_faster: Per the benchmark text: the substitution and search wins use SymbolicUtils' IRStructure acceleration structure, which visits shared subexpressions once; the compiled-call win is a native Julia function produced by Code.toexpr plus eval (JIT compiled), against SymEngine's LambdaRealDoubleVisitor, which the file describes as 'an interpreter over the expression tree'.
tradeoffs: The JIT path pays a large setup cost: codegen init is 12x slower than SymEngine's. Core operations (expand, differentiate, series, deep evaluation) are 10-48x slower than SymEngine in this run.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the Symbolics/SciML maintainers, single run without variance. The file itself says the first workload set 'plays to SymEngine's strengths' and the second set is SymbolicUtils-native; for substitution and search rows the SymbolicUtils column is the faster of two variants (plain and IRStructure-backed). The SymEngine 'variable search' is free_symbols accumulation into a set, not an identical operation. The compiled-call row excludes the 12x higher compile cost. The C++ build flags of SymEngine_jll are not stated, so the baseline's optimisation level is unknown.

name: EvoTrees.jl (Julia gradient-boosted trees) vs XGBoost hist (C++, CPU and GPU)
baseline: XGBoost v3.1.2 (C++/CUDA, 'hist' algorithm) driven from Julia through XGBoost.jl
workload: Regression boosted trees on random Matrix{Float64}, 200 iterations, nobs 100k/1M/10M, nfeats 10/100, max_depth 6/11; training and inference seconds on CPU (12 threads) and GPU.
claimed_speedup: No headline claim; README tables only. CPU training is faster only at 10M rows x 10 features (26.45 s vs 30.99 s at depth 6, 51.88 s vs 55.20 s at depth 11; 1.17x and 1.06x derived from page data), equal at 100k x 100 depth 6 (0.79 s both), and slower elsewhere (for example 192.58 s vs 111.69 s at 10M x 100 depth 11, 0.36 s vs 0.21 s at 100k x 10 depth 6); CPU inference is slower in every row. GPU: EvoTrees trains faster at depth 11 with 100 features (2.17 s vs 2.92 s at 100k, 5.07 s vs 6.80 s at 1M, 37.25 s vs 41.98 s at 10M) and infers faster in those rows (0.32 s vs 0.58 s at 1M, 3.57 s vs 5.91 s at 10M); GPU is slower at depth 6 and with 10 features.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.10.8, EvoTrees v0.18.3, XGBoost v3.1.2 hist; XGBoost build flags are not stated (prebuilt binary via Julia packages). Script: benchmarks/regressor.jl.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5900X (12 threads) and NVIDIA RTX A4000
tradeoffs: Slower than XGBoost in most CPU rows and all CPU inference rows; supports multi-target and maximum-likelihood objectives natively in Julia.
caveats: The README does not claim to beat XGBoost; the wins are read off its own table. Models are trained on random data and model quality or equal tree structure is not compared. XGBoost thread and GPU options other than hist are not listed. Whether Julia compilation time is inside the timings is not stated. One machine, no variance reported.

name: Ripserer.jl (Julia persistent homology) vs Ripser and Cubical Ripser (C++)
baseline: Ripser (C++, master commit 286d369) and Cubical Ripser (C++, commits 6edb9c5 for 2D and a063dac for 3D)
workload: Persistent homology of Vietoris-Rips filtrations (datasets from the Ripser paper and PH-roadmap, parsed as Float32, parse time included) and of cubical image filtrations; minimum of five runs.
claimed_speedup: Docs: 'very close to Ripser, usually within around 30%' and 'on very sparse inputs ... can sometimes outperform Ripser'. Ripserer/Ripser time ratios from the page: Alpha-Rips 0.807 (636 ms vs 789 ms), 0.741 (872 ms vs 1.179 s), 0.744 (56 ms vs 76 ms), 0.942 (5.844 s vs 6.203 s) and 1.058 (49.431 s vs 46.707 s, slower); sparse=true mode 0.993 and 0.998 on o3_1024 and o3_4096, 0.932 on random16, but 1.267 on dragon2000 and 1.304 on fract-r; dense mode is slower on 5 of 6 sets (ratio 1.04 to 1.99, o3_4096 151.5 s vs 76.2 s) with random16 at 0.803. Versus Cubical Ripser: 0.96 on bonsai64 (2.875 s vs 2.996 s), slower elsewhere (up to 2.631).
compiler_and_flags: Ripserer v0.15 (Julia version not stated); Ripser and Cubical Ripser built from the stated master commits, compiler and flags not stated. Code and datasets: github.com/mtsch/RipsererBenchmarks.jl.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i5-4200U @ 1.60GHz and 8 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Uses more memory than Ripser on small inputs (heap includes the Julia runtime, for example 138 MiB vs 33 MiB on alpha_3_sphere_3000) but supports higher-dimensional cubical complexes, critical simplices and representative cycles.
caveats: Mostly parity or slower; wins of about 1.05-1.35x appear only on very sparse Alpha-Rips inputs and in a few tiny cases, and the docs give no mechanism for them (the shared tricks, implicit complex and clearing, are the same as Ripser's). Author's own benchmark on an old dual-core laptop with a 2020-era Ripserer v0.15 and 2020 Ripser commits, so the page may be stale. Ripser build flags are not stated.
found_via: Julia General registry candidate (mtsch). Opened raw docs/src/index.md and docs/src/benchmarks.md of Ripserer.jl and the RipsererBenchmarks.jl README, plus github.com repo and commits pages.

name: Julia vs C++ (clang, CMake Release): aaronang/stl-benchmark ParseStl
baseline: C++ ParseStl benchmark (Google Benchmark) built with clang++ and CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
workload: Parse the file nist.stl (the README does not define the STL format) once per iteration; C++ reports CPU time over 1729 iterations, Julia reports @btime.
claimed_speedup: C++ 409.210 us, Julia 211.641 us, Python 25150.9 us: Julia about 1.93x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: clang/clang++ (version not stated) via CMake Release; Julia v1.0 started with `julia -O3`
hardware: Only the C++ run lists the machine: '8 X 2300 MHz CPU s', L1 32K, L2 262K, L3 6291K (CPU model not named); the Julia run's hardware is not stated
tradeoffs: Single small parsing kernel written by the repo author in each language.
caveats: Author says 'I am neither a C++ nor Julia expert' and asks readers to report inefficient implementations. The two timings come from different tools (Google Benchmark CPU time vs BenchmarkTools @btime) and possibly different machines; the C++ and Julia parsers were not compared for equal work or allocation behaviour, and the explanatory blog post is on github.io (blocked here). Julia 1.0 from 2018.

name: LowRankApprox.jl (Julia randomized interpolative decomposition) vs SciPy/Fortran ID
baseline: SciPy interpolative decomposition (scipy.linalg.interpolative, which calls a Fortran backend; README links PyMatrixID); the README also names MATLAB
workload: Interpolative decomposition (ID) of a 1024 x 1024 Hilbert matrix to relative precision about 1e-15.
claimed_speedup: README: ~0.02 s with LowRankApprox in Julia vs ~0.07 s with SciPy (Fortran backend) and ~0.3 s in MATLAB, i.e. about 3.5x faster than SciPy (derived from page data); the README also says 'large speedups over similar codes written in MATLAB and Python (and even some in Fortran and C)'.
why_faster: README: 'in part both algorithmic improvements as well as ... low-level optimizations' (the package uses an early-terminating pivoted-QR based ID rather than the Fortran library's algorithm).
tradeoffs: Randomized, early-terminating approximation; works on BLAS/LAPACK-compatible matrices and matrix-free operators.
caveats: Single approximate figure per language with no hardware, Julia, SciPy or compiler versions, no benchmark script, and 'early tests' from the package's 2015-2016 origin. The baseline is a Python wrapper over Fortran, not C or C++ at -O3, and the README attributes the gap partly to a different algorithm. The 'even some in Fortran and C' claim has no numbers.
